claim: When fed live E. coli strain OP50, all hatched C. elegans larvae develop to adults within 3 days at 20°C.
source: When fed live E. coli strain OP50, a standard laboratory food for C. elegans, all hatched larvae develop to adults within 3 days at 20°C.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental results described in the manuscript.

claim: Worms fed heat-killed OP50 (HK-OP50) arrested development at early larval stages (L1-L2) and failed to consume the bacterial lawn.
source: However, when worms were fed OP50 that was killed by heat treatment (75°C for 90 min; HK-OP50 hereafter), they arrested development at early larval stages (L1-L2) and failed to consume the bacterial lawn (Figure 1A)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A, including microscope images and bar graphs.

claim: Heat-killed bacteria lack certain nutrients or molecules required for C. elegans larval growth.
source: However, when worms were fed OP50 that was killed by heat treatment (75°C for 90 min; HK-OP50 hereafter), they arrested development at early larval stages (L1-L2) and failed to consume the bacterial lawn (Figure 1A), suggesting that the heat-killed bacteria lacked certain nutrients or molecules required for larval growth
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observed developmental arrest and lack of food consumption.

claim: E. coli contains heat-labile nutrients required for C. elegans normal growth and longevity.
source: suggesting that the heat-killed bacteria lacked certain nutrients or molecules required for larval growth, which is consistent with published observation suggesting that E. coli contains heat-labile nutrients required for C.elegans normal growth and longevity (Lenaerts et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous published work.

claim: Wild-type worms demonstrated a strong discrimination against HK-OP50 in food dwelling and food choice assays.
source: We performed two behavior assays to assess food dwelling and food choice (Brandt and Ringstad, 2015; Fujiwara et al., 2002; Kniazeva et al., 2015; Melo and Ruvkun, 2012; Shtonda and Avery, 2006). The results demonstrated a strong discrimination against HK-OP50 by wild-type worms (Figure 1B and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from behavioral assays shown in Figures 1B and C.

claim: In the food choice assay, live OP50 lawn was favored until it was consumed at day 4, when most worms then moved to the HK-OP50 and consumed that lawn.
source: Interestingly, in the food choice assay, the live OP50 lawn was favored until it was consumed at day 4, when most worms then moved to the HK-OP50 and consumed that lawn (Figure 1C)
evidence: This is a direct observation from the food choice assay data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Worms eat heat-killed bacteria if they have first obtained some benefit from live bacteria.
source: Interestingly, in the food choice assay, the live OP50 lawn was favored until it was consumed at day 4, when most worms then moved to the HK-OP50 and consumed that lawn (Figure 1C), suggesting that worms eat heat-killed bacteria if they have first obtained some benefit from live bacteria.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observed behavior in the food choice assay.

claim: When live-OP50 was added to worms grown on HK-OP50 plate for 30 days, they recovered to adults with viable progeny.
source: Moreover, when live-OP50 was added to worms grown on HK-OP50 plate for 30 days, they recovered to adults with viable progeny (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A)
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental results shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Nutrient deficiency in HK-OP50 induced a protective response from the worms similar to starvation response.
source: Moreover, when live-OP50 was added to worms grown on HK-OP50 plate for 30 days, they recovered to adults with viable progeny (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), suggesting nutrient deficiency in HK-OP50 induced a protective response from the worms similar to starvation response.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that worms can recover after prolonged exposure to HK-OP50.

claim: When eggs were placed on HK-OP50 lawn containing a tiny amount of live Staphylococcus saprophyticus (SS), the hatched worms were able to consume HK-OP50 and grow.
source: When eggs were placed on HK-OP50 lawn containing a tiny amount of live SS, the hatched worms were able to consume HK-OP50 and grow, suggesting that the live bacteria provided micronutrients that rendered the heat-killed bacteria edible (Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental results shown in Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Live bacteria provided micronutrients that rendered the heat-killed bacteria edible.
source: When eggs were placed on HK-OP50 lawn containing a tiny amount of live SS, the hatched worms were able to consume HK-OP50 and grow, suggesting that the live bacteria provided micronutrients that rendered the heat-killed bacteria edible (Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that a small amount of live bacteria enables worms to consume HK-OP50.

claim: The potential components from live bacteria did not reach the worms through odorants.
source: Additional tests indicated that such potential components did not reach the worms through odorants and suggested that worms likely obtain the benefit from the small amount live bacteria through ingestion (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C; Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Worms likely obtain the benefit from the small amount of live bacteria through ingestion.
source: Additional tests indicated that such potential components did not reach the worms through odorants and suggested that worms likely obtain the benefit from the small amount live bacteria through ingestion (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C; Figure 1C).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data.

claim: The trace amount of live bacteria, ingested by the worms, stayed in the intestine and continuously secreted micronutrients into the gut tract, similar to microbes in mammalian gut.
source: These data led to a speculative model that the trace amount of live bacteria, ingested by the worms, stayed in the intestine and continuously secreted micronutrients into the gut tract, which is similar to microbes in mammalian gut.
evidence: This is explicitly stated as a speculative model based on the experimental observations.

claim: Vitamin B2 (VB2) supplementation partially but significantly recovered larval growth as indicated by increased gonad length at day 7.
source: Among micronutrients tested, we found that vitamin B2 (VB2) supplementation partially but significantly recovered larval growth as indicated by increased gonad length at day 7, which indicated the increased usage of the food (Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: VB2 supplementation does not completely compensate for the undefined deficiencies of heat-killed bacteria.
source: These animals fed VB2 supplemented food still grew very slowly, reaching mid to late larval stages based on gonad length and vulval development compared to that of well-fed worms, but never reach adulthood by day 7 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B,C). This slow growth indicated that VB2 supplementation does not completely compensate for the undefined deficiencies of heat-killed bacteria
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that worms fed VB2-supplemented HK-OP50 still grow slowly.

claim: Multiple essential nutrients are lacking in heat-killed bacteria.
source: This slow growth indicated that VB2 supplementation does not completely compensate for the undefined deficiencies of heat-killed bacteria, which suggested that multiple essential nutrients are lacking in heat-killed bacteria.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the incomplete recovery of growth with VB2 supplementation.

claim: VB2 may play a critical role in a food-quality evaluation pathway.
source: However, the prominent increase in growth suggested that VB2 may play a critical role in a food-quality evaluation pathway.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the significant effect of VB2 supplementation on growth.

claim: VB2 supplementation increased the preference for heat-killed bacteria.
source: Our behavior assays showed that VB2 supplementation increased the preference for heat-killed bacteria (Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from behavior assays shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 2A.

claim: The VB2 level was drastically reduced in worms fed HK-OP50, compared to worms fed live OP50.
source: Using HPLC-UV (Howe et al., 2015), we found the VB2 level was drastically reduced in worms fed HK-OP50, compared to worms fed live OP50, and the level was mostly recovered by VB2 supplementation (Figure 2C)
evidence: This is supported by HPLC-UV analysis data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: VB2 level in worms fed HK-OP50 was mostly recovered by VB2 supplementation.
source: Using HPLC-UV (Howe et al., 2015), we found the VB2 level was drastically reduced in worms fed HK-OP50, compared to worms fed live OP50, and the level was mostly recovered by VB2 supplementation (Figure 2C)
evidence: This is supported by HPLC-UV analysis data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: VB2 was very low in heat-killed bacteria.
source: Using HPLC-UV (Howe et al., 2015), we found the VB2 level was drastically reduced in worms fed HK-OP50, compared to worms fed live OP50, and the level was mostly recovered by VB2 supplementation (Figure 2C), suggesting VB2 was very low in heat-killed bacteria.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the reduced VB2 levels in worms fed HK-OP50.

claim: VB2 level is low in heat-killed OP50.
source: To confirm this, we measured the VB2 level in bacteria and found that VB2 level is low in heat-killed OP50 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is supported by direct measurement of VB2 in bacteria shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Larval growth was enhanced only by protease-treated HK-OP50.
source: To understand how VB2 affects food uptake in worms, we tested the role of the digestive system by feeding worms with HK-OP50 culture pre-treated with exogenous digestive enzymes. We found that larval growth was enhanced only by protease-treated HK-OP50 (Figure 2D)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Exogenous protein digestion improved usability of the heat-killed bacteria.
source: We found that larval growth was enhanced only by protease-treated HK-OP50 (Figure 2D), indicating that exogenous protein digestion improved usability of the heat-killed bacteria.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that protease treatment enhances growth.

claim: HK-OP50 supplemented with a protease inhibitor cocktail (PIC) eliminated the beneficial effect of VB2 supplementation.
source: We then observed that HK-OP50 supplemented with a protease inhibitor cocktail (PIC) eliminated the beneficial effect of VB2 supplementation (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Worms fed HK-OP50 have reduced protease activity.
source: These results suggest that worms fed HK-OP50 have reduced protease activity, and that the benefit of VB2 supplementation is dependent on endogenous proteases.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the enzyme treatment and protease inhibitor experiments.

claim: The benefit of VB2 supplementation is dependent on endogenous proteases.
source: These results suggest that worms fed HK-OP50 have reduced protease activity, and that the benefit of VB2 supplementation is dependent on endogenous proteases.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the protease inhibitor experiment.

claim: The protease activity was drastically reduced in worms fed HK-OP50, compared to worms fed live OP50.
source: We then used a protease detection assay (Hama et al., 2009; Semova et al., 2012) to directly examine the in vivo protease activity in the intestinal tract (Figure 2—figure supplement 2D and E). We found that the protease activity was drastically reduced in worms fed HK-OP50, compared to worms fed live OP50, and VB2 supplementation partially recovered the protease activity (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is supported by in vivo protease activity assay data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: VB2 supplementation partially recovered the protease activity in worms fed HK-OP50.
source: We found that the protease activity was drastically reduced in worms fed HK-OP50, compared to worms fed live OP50, and VB2 supplementation partially recovered the protease activity (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is supported by in vivo protease activity assay data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Worms down-regulate digestive enzymes in response to VB2 deficiency.
source: Taken together, these data support that worms down-regulate digestive enzymes in response to VB2 deficiency.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined experimental results on protease activity.

claim: The mRNA levels of asp-13, asp-14, cpr-1 and cpr-4 were dramatically increased in worms fed HK-OP50+VB2 compared to that in worms fed HK-OP50.
source: To identify the proteases regulated by VB2, we examined the mRNA levels of 27 intestine-enriched, protease genes (McGhee et al., 2007). qRT-PCR analysis showed that the mRNA levels of four genes, asp-13, asp-14, cpr-1 and cpr-4, were dramatically increased in worms fed HK-OP50+VB2 compared to that in worms fed HK-OP50 (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR analysis data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Among asp-13, asp-14, cpr-1 and cpr-4, asp-13 and asp-14 were also highly expressed in worms fed on live bacteria.
source: Among these four genes, asp-13 and asp-14 were also highly expressed in worms fed on live bacteria (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR analysis data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Knocking down both asp-13 and asp-14 resulted in a strong suppression of the effect of VB2 supplementation.
source: We then found that knocking down both asp-13 and asp-14 resulted in a strong suppression of the effect of VB2 supplementation (Figure 3B)
evidence: This is supported by RNAi experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: ASP-13 and ASP-14 are essential for the VB2 effect.
source: We then found that knocking down both asp-13 and asp-14 resulted in a strong suppression of the effect of VB2 supplementation (Figure 3B), suggesting that these enzymes are essential for the VB2 effect.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the RNAi knockdown experiment.

claim: Over-expression of both asp-13 and asp-14 behind a ubiquitously expressed rpl-28 promoter significantly improved the food uptake and dwelling behavior of worms fed HK-OP50.
source: Over-expression of both asp-13 and asp-14 behind a ubiquitously expressed rpl-28 promoter (termed asp-13/14 OE) (Zhang et al., 2009) significantly improved the food uptake and dwelling behavior of worms fed HK-OP50, as determined by the gonad length, food choice and seeking assays (Figure 3C–E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3C-E.

claim: Intestinal-specific RNAi of asp-13/14 prevents the rescue effect of VB2 supplementation on worms fed HK-food.
source: Moreover, intestinal-specific RNAi of asp-13/14 prevents the rescue effect of VB2 supplementation on worms fed HK-food (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B)
evidence: This is supported by intestinal-specific RNAi experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: Intestinal function of ASP-13 and ASP14 are essential for the VB2 effect.
source: Moreover, intestinal-specific RNAi of asp-13/14 prevents the rescue effect of VB2 supplementation on worms fed HK-food (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B), suggesting that intestinal function of ASP-13 and ASP14 are essential for the VB2 effect.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the intestinal-specific RNAi experiment.

claim: asp-13/14 is highly expressed in the intestine.
source: This is consistent with the previous finding that asp-13/14 is highly expressed in the intestine (McGhee et al., 2007)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous published work.

claim: ASP-13 and ASP-14 play a critical role in the VB2-induced increase in protease activity and uptake of heat-killed bacteria.
source: These data strongly support a critical role of ASP-13 and ASP-14 in the VB2-induced increase in protease activity and uptake of heat-killed bacteria.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined experimental results on asp-13 and asp-14.

claim: The protease activity was most dramatically decreased in worms treated with elt-2(RNAi).
source: To identify transcription factors that regulate the expression of intestinal protease genes in response to VB2 supplementation, we combined RNAi with the protease assay to screen 18 transcription factors previously shown to be enriched in the intestine (McGhee et al., 2007) (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A). The protease activity was most dramatically decreased in worms treated with elt-2(RNAi) (Figure 3F and Figure 3—figure supplement 2A)
evidence: This is supported by RNAi screen data shown in Figure 3F and Figure 3—figure supplement 2A.

claim: elt-2(RNAi) decreases the expression of ~50% of known protease genes, including asp-13 and asp-14.
source: The protease activity was most dramatically decreased in worms treated with elt-2(RNAi) (Figure 3F and Figure 3—figure supplement 2A), which is consistent with the recent report that elt-2(RNAi) decreases the expression of ~50% of known protease genes, including asp-13 and asp-14 (Mann et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a recent published report.

claim: The ELT-2::GFP signal was decreased in worms fed HK-OP50 and the reduction was mostly recovered by VB2 supplementation.
source: Using an integrated, translational ELT-2::GFP reporter strain which is in a glo-4 mutant background to reduce auto fluorescence (Mann et al., 2016), we found that the ELT-2::GFP signal was decreased in worms fed HK-OP50 and the reduction was mostly recovered by VB2 supplementation (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence imaging data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Decreased ELT-2 on heat-killed food was recovered by VB2 supplementation in wild-type worm.
source: We also found that decreased ELT-2 on heat-killed food was recovered by VB2 supplementation in wild-type worm (Figure 3G, Western blot)
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: ELT-2 expression responds to changes in nutrient status.
source: We also found that decreased ELT-2 on heat-killed food was recovered by VB2 supplementation in wild-type worm (Figure 3G, Western blot), supporting that ELT-2 expression responds to changes in nutrient status.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observed changes in ELT-2 expression under different feeding conditions.

claim: Over-expression of ELT-2 significantly increased both larval growth measured by gonad length and protease activity in worms fed HK-OP50.
source: Using an established ELT-2 over-expression [elt-2 (OE)] strain (Mann et al., 2016), we found that over-expression of ELT-2 significantly increased both larval growth measured by gonad length and protease activity in worms fed HK-OP50, eliminated the preference for HK-OP50+VB2 over HK-OP50 in the food choice assay, and increased the expression of asp-13 and asp-14 (Figure 3H and I; Figure 3—figure supplement 2B and C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3H, 3I, and Figure 3—figure supplement 2B and C.

claim: Over-expression of ELT-2 eliminated the preference for HK-OP50+VB2 over HK-OP50 in the food choice assay.
source: Using an established ELT-2 over-expression [elt-2 (OE)] strain (Mann et al., 2016), we found that over-expression of ELT-2 significantly increased both larval growth measured by gonad length and protease activity in worms fed HK-OP50, eliminated the preference for HK-OP50+VB2 over HK-OP50 in the food choice assay, and increased the expression of asp-13 and asp-14 (Figure 3H and I; Figure 3—figure supplement 2B and C).
evidence: This is supported by food choice assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Over-expression of ELT-2 increased the expression of asp-13 and asp-14.
source: Using an established ELT-2 over-expression [elt-2 (OE)] strain (Mann et al., 2016), we found that over-expression of ELT-2 significantly increased both larval growth measured by gonad length and protease activity in worms fed HK-OP50, eliminated the preference for HK-OP50+VB2 over HK-OP50 in the food choice assay, and increased the expression of asp-13 and asp-14 (Figure 3H and I; Figure 3—figure supplement 2B and C).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Increased expression of elt-2 is both necessary and sufficient for the impact of VB2 on protease expression and food usability.
source: Therefore, increased expression of elt-2 is both necessary and sufficient for the impact of VB2 on protease expression and food usability.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined experimental results on ELT-2.

claim: Down-regulating asp-13 and asp-14 by a low ELT-2 level critically contributes to the poor food usage in worms fed HK-OP50.
source: Additional tests supported the hypothesis that down-regulating asp-13 and asp-14 by a low ELT-2 level critically contributes to the poor food usage in worms fed HK-OP50 (Figure 3—figure supplement 2D and E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2D and E.

claim: Pretreatment with RNAi targeting either daf-15/raptor or ragc-1 essentially eliminated the effect of VB2 supplementation on protease activity.
source: We first tested if TORC1 is required for VB2-induced activation of digestive enzymes in worms fed heat-killed bacteria. We found that pretreatment with RNAi targeting either daf-15/raptor or ragc-1, encoding two key TORC1 components (Jia et al., 2004; Long et al., 2002; Robida-Stubbs et al., 2012), essentially eliminated the effect of VB2 supplementation on protease activity (Figure 4A)
evidence: This is supported by RNAi experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: VB2 induction of protease activity is TORC1 dependent.
source: We found that pretreatment with RNAi targeting either daf-15/raptor or ragc-1, encoding two key TORC1 components (Jia et al., 2004; Long et al., 2002; Robida-Stubbs et al., 2012), essentially eliminated the effect of VB2 supplementation on protease activity (Figure 4A), indicating that VB2 induction of protease activity is TORC1 dependent.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the RNAi experiment targeting TORC1 components.

claim: Protease activity is not all reduced in arrested larvae.
source: To address that lower TORC1 activity on protease activity derive does not simply from slowing or arresting development, we tested the protease activity of several arrested larvae (RNAi treatment). Figure 4—figure supplement 1 shows that protease activity is not all reduced in arrested larvae
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Lower TORC1 activity on protease activity is unlikely to be from generally slowing or arresting development.
source: Figure 4—figure supplement 1 shows that protease activity is not all reduced in arrested larvae, which indicate that lower TORC1 activity on protease activity (Figure 4A) is unlikely to be from generally slowing or arresting development.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that protease activity is not uniformly reduced in arrested larvae.

claim: Worms fed HK-OP50 displayed a high level of LGG-1::GFP puncta in seam cells compared to that in worms fed live OP50.
source: We then measured TORC1 activity by utilizing an established autophagy marker (LGG-1::GFP puncta) known to be repressed by TORC1 (Robida-Stubbs et al., 2012). We found that worms fed HK-OP50 displayed a high level of LGG-1::GFP puncta in seam cells compared to that in worms fed live OP50, and this increase was suppressed by VB2 supplementation (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by autophagy marker data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The increase in LGG-1::GFP puncta in worms fed HK-OP50 was suppressed by VB2 supplementation.
source: We found that worms fed HK-OP50 displayed a high level of LGG-1::GFP puncta in seam cells compared to that in worms fed live OP50, and this increase was suppressed by VB2 supplementation (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by autophagy marker data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The elevated LGG-1::GFP puncta level in worms fed HK-OP50 was suppressed by hyperactivation of TORC1 in a nprl-3 loss-of-function (lf) mutant.
source: To support that the observed change in the LGG-1::GFP puncta level under our testing conditions reflects a specific change in TORC1 activity, we showed that the elevated LGG-1::GFP puncta level in worms fed HK-OP50 was suppressed by hyperactivation of TORC1 in a nprl-3 loss-of-function (lf) mutant (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A.

claim: NPRL-3 is a negative regulator of TORC1 in both worms and mammalian cells.
source: NPRL-3 is a negative regulator of TORC1 in both worms and mammalian cells (Bar-Peled et al., 2013; Zhu et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published work.

claim: Inhibition of TORC1 activity by daf-15(RNAi) elevated the LGG-1::GFP puncta level in well-fed, young larvae.
source: Conversely, inhibition of TORC1 activity by daf-15(RNAi) elevated the LGG-1::GFP puncta level in well-fed, young larvae (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Apical localization of VHA-6 was altered in worms fed HK-OP50 and this defect was suppressed by VB2 supplementation.
source: In addition, apical localization of VHA-6, which we previously showed contributes to intestinal TORC1 activation by a lipid biosynthesis pathway (Zhu et al., 2015), was altered in worms fed HK-OP50 and this defect was suppressed by VB2 supplementation (Figure 4—figure supplement 2C and D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2C and D.

claim: TORC1 activity is decreased in worms fed heat-killed bacteria.
source: These data indicate that TORC1 activity is decreased in worms fed heat-killed bacteria and that VB2 supplementation significantly recovers the activity.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined experimental results on TORC1 activity markers.

claim: VB2 supplementation significantly recovers TORC1 activity in worms fed heat-killed bacteria.
source: These data indicate that TORC1 activity is decreased in worms fed heat-killed bacteria and that VB2 supplementation significantly recovers the activity.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined experimental results on TORC1 activity markers.

claim: TORC1 acts downstream of VB2.
source: We obtained further evidence that TORC1 acts downstream of VB2 by showing that TORC1 activation is sufficient to mimic the effect of VB2 in boosting intestinal protease activity and food usage.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results showing that TORC1 activation mimics VB2 effects.

claim: The nprl-3(lf) mutation significantly improved intestinal protease activity, the expression of asp-13 and asp-14, larval growth measured by gonad length and dwelling behavior of worms fed HK-OP50.
source: Specifically, we found that the nprl-3(lf) mutation significantly improved intestinal protease activity, the expression of asp-13 and asp-14, larval growth measured by gonad length and dwelling behavior of worms fed HK-OP50 (Figure 4C–G)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 4C-G.

claim: The rescue by nprl-3(lf) was not because VB2 level was recovered as VB2 level in nprl-3 (lf) mutants fed heat-killed food did not increase.
source: however, this rescue was not because VB2 level was recovered as VB2 level in nprl-3 (lf) mutants fed heat-killed food did not increase (Figure 4—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: This is supported by HPLC-UV analysis data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2E.

claim: Reducing TORC1 activity (daf-15 RNAi) led to defects in food choice.
source: In contrast, reducing TORC1 activity (daf-15 RNAi) led to defects in food choice (Figure 4—figure supplement 2F).
evidence: This is supported by food choice assay data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2F.

claim: daf-15(RNAi) treatment decreased the expression of the translational ELT-2::GFP reporter in the reporter strain and the endogenous ELT-2 protein in the wild-type.
source: Moreover, daf-15(RNAi) treatment decreased the expression of the translational ELT-2::GFP reporter in the reporter strain and the endogenous ELT-2 protein in the wild-type (Figure 4—figure supplement 2G)
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence imaging and Western blot data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2G.

claim: TORC1 mediates the effect of VB2 on the expression of proteases and the usage of heat-killed bacteria.
source: Therefore, our data strongly support that TORC1 mediates the effect of VB2 on the expression of proteases and the usage of heat-killed bacteria.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined experimental results on TORC1.

claim: Vitamin B2, also known as riboflavin, is the precursor of flavin mononucleotide (FMN) and flavin adenine dinucleotide (FAD).
source: Vitamin B2, also known as riboflavin, is the precursor of flavin mononucleotide (FMN) and flavin adenine dinucleotide (FAD) (Joosten and van Berkel, 2007; Lienhart et al., 2013; Powers, 2003) (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Both FMN and FAD levels were decreased in worms fed HK-OP50 compared to worms fed live OP50.
source: Using HPLC-UV analysis, we found that both FMN and FAD levels were decreased in worms fed HK-OP50 compared to worms fed live OP50, and their levels were partially restored by VB2 supplementation (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by HPLC-UV analysis data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: FMN and FAD levels were partially restored by VB2 supplementation in worms fed HK-OP50.
source: Using HPLC-UV analysis, we found that both FMN and FAD levels were decreased in worms fed HK-OP50 compared to worms fed live OP50, and their levels were partially restored by VB2 supplementation (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by HPLC-UV analysis data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Lack of sufficient FAD and FMN likely contributes to the low quality of heat-killed bacteria as a food source.
source: Therefore, lack of sufficient FAD and FMN likely contributes to the low quality of heat-killed bacteria as a food source.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observed decreases in FMN and FAD levels.

claim: FAD supplementation improved food uptake, intestinal protease activity and ELT-2 expression, as VB2 does.
source: To test if FAD also mediates the VB2 impact on TORC1 and protease production, we showed that FAD supplementation improved food uptake, intestinal protease activity and ELT-2 expression, as VB2 does (Figure 5C and D; Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 5C, 5D, and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The FAD benefit is TORC1 dependent, as pretreatment with RNAi targeting daf-15/raptor essentially eliminated the effect of FAD supplementation on protease activity.
source: Furthermore, the FAD benefit is also TORC1 dependent, as pretreatment with RNAi targeting daf-15/raptor essentially eliminated the effect of FAD supplementation on protease activity (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by RNAi experimental data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Protease activity was dramatically reduced in both flad-1(RNAi) and rft-2(RNAi) treated strains.
source: We then further analyzed the functional relationship between FAD and TORC1 by decreasing FAD production through RNAi of a FAD synthetase gene (flad-1) and a riboflavin transporter gene (rft-2) (Biswas et al., 2013; Gandhimathi et al., 2015; Liuzzi et al., 2012) (Figure 5A). Protease activity was dramatically reduced in both RNAi-treated strains and the activity was recovered in nprl-3(lf) mutants (Figure 5E,F,H and I).
evidence: This is supported by RNAi experimental data shown in Figures 5E, 5F, 5H, and 5I.

claim: Protease activity in flad-1(RNAi) and rft-2(RNAi) treated strains was recovered in nprl-3(lf) mutants.
source: Protease activity was dramatically reduced in both RNAi-treated strains and the activity was recovered in nprl-3(lf) mutants (Figure 5E,F,H and I).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 5E, 5F, 5H, and 5I.

claim: Both flad-1(RNAi) and rft-2(RNAi) significantly increased autophagy.
source: Furthermore, both flad-1(RNAi) and rft-2(RNAi) significantly increased autophagy (Figure 5G and J).
evidence: This is supported by autophagy marker data shown in Figures 5G and 5J.

claim: TORC1 acts downstream of FAD to promote protease activity.
source: These data support that TORC1 acts downstream of FAD to promote protease activity.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined experimental results on FAD and TORC1.

claim: FAD plays the key role in mediating VB2 effect on intestinal protease activity.
source: The similarity of the data between flad-1 and rft-2 further supports that FAD plays the key role in mediating VB2 effect on intestinal protease activity.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the similarity of results between flad-1 and rft-2 RNAi.

claim: FAD-associated proteins are involved in many metabolic events including fatty acid metabolism, the TCA cycle and electron transport chain.
source: FAD-associated proteins are involved in many metabolic events including fatty acid metabolism, the TCA cycle and electron transport chain (Lienhart et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: TORC1 is known to be an ATP sensor in mammals and C. elegans.
source: Since many of these events are related to energy production, and TORC1 is known to be an ATP sensor in mammals and C. elegans (Chin et al., 2014; Dennis et al., 2001; Hay and Sonenberg, 2004)
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The ATP level was dramatically reduced in worms fed HK-OP50 compared to that in worms fed live OP50.
source: We found that the ATP level was indeed dramatically reduced in worms fed HK-OP50 compared to that in worms fed live OP50, whereas VB2/FAD supplementation partially recovered the level (Figure 5K).
evidence: This is supported by ATP measurement data shown in Figure 5K.

claim: VB2/FAD supplementation partially recovered the ATP level in worms fed HK-OP50.
source: We found that the ATP level was indeed dramatically reduced in worms fed HK-OP50 compared to that in worms fed live OP50, whereas VB2/FAD supplementation partially recovered the level (Figure 5K).
evidence: This is supported by ATP measurement data shown in Figure 5K.

claim: Reducing FAD production by flad-1(RNAi) in the first generation of wild-type worms reduced ATP and the reduction was eliminated by FAD supplementation.
source: Consistently, reducing FAD production by flad-1(RNAi) in the first generation of wild-type worms also reduced ATP and the reduction was eliminated by FAD supplementation (Figure 5K).
evidence: This is supported by ATP measurement data shown in Figure 5K.

claim: The decreased ATP level is a major cellular consequence of VB2 deficiency.
source: Therefore, the decreased ATP level is a major cellular consequence of VB2 deficiency.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observed ATP level changes under VB2 deficiency.

claim: A modest reduction of ATP level was observed in the first generation of atp-2(RNAi)-treated animals.
source: To provide further evidence that ATP reduction is causal to the reduction in TORC1 and protease activity, we used RNAi to partially inactivate atp-2/ATP5B that encodes an ATP synthetase known to affect ATP production in worms (Chin et al., 2014). We also observed a modest reduction of ATP level in the first generation of atp-2(RNAi)-treated animals and the reduction was not overcome by FAD supplementation (Figure 5K)
evidence: This is supported by ATP measurement data shown in Figure 5K.

claim: The ATP reduction in atp-2(RNAi)-treated animals was not overcome by FAD supplementation.
source: We also observed a modest reduction of ATP level in the first generation of atp-2(RNAi)-treated animals and the reduction was not overcome by FAD supplementation (Figure 5K), consistent with atp-2 acting downstream of FAD regarding ATP production.
evidence: This is supported by ATP measurement data shown in Figure 5K.

claim: atp-2 acts downstream of FAD regarding ATP production.
source: We also observed a modest reduction of ATP level in the first generation of atp-2(RNAi)-treated animals and the reduction was not overcome by FAD supplementation (Figure 5K), consistent with atp-2 acting downstream of FAD regarding ATP production.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that FAD supplementation does not overcome ATP reduction in atp-2(RNAi) animals.

claim: Intestinal protease activity was prominently decreased in the second generation of atp-2(RNAi)-treated animals.
source: Importantly, intestinal protease activity was prominently decreased in the second generation of atp-2(RNAi)-treated animals and the reduction was partially suppressed by nprl-3(lf) (Figure 5L and M).
evidence: This is supported by protease activity assay data shown in Figures 5L and 5M.

claim: The reduction in protease activity in atp-2(RNAi)-treated animals was partially suppressed by nprl-3(lf).
source: Importantly, intestinal protease activity was prominently decreased in the second generation of atp-2(RNAi)-treated animals and the reduction was partially suppressed by nprl-3(lf) (Figure 5L and M).
evidence: This is supported by protease activity assay data shown in Figures 5L and 5M.

claim: LGG-1::GFP puncta were increased in atp-2(RNAi) worms fed live OP50.
source: Furthermore, LGG-1::GFP puncta were increased in atp-2(RNAi) worms fed live OP50 (Figure 5N), which is consistent with a previous observation in C. elegans (Chin et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by autophagy marker data shown in Figure 5N.

claim: The ATP level change mediates the impact of VB2 on TORC1 and intestinal protease activity.
source: Together, these data support the hypothesis that the ATP level change mediates the impact of VB2 on TORC1 and intestinal protease activity.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined experimental results on ATP, TORC1, and protease activity.

claim: The study does not exclude potential impacts of other metabolic products from FAD-associated enzymes in the process.
source: Our data do not exclude potential impacts of other metabolic products from FAD-associated enzymes in the process.
evidence: This is an explicit acknowledgment of the limitations of the study.

claim: The study identified an intestinal food-quality evaluation mechanism by which animals detect vitamin B2 deficiency by the FAD-ATP-TORC1-ELT-2 pathway that dictates food uptake and foraging behaviors.
source: We identified an intestinal food-quality evaluation mechanism by which animals detect vitamin B2 deficiency by the FAD-ATP-TORC1-ELT-2 pathway that dictates food uptake and foraging behaviors (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, summarizing the identified pathway.

claim: Such a mechanism with conserved functions enhances survival in wild environments by discriminating against low-quality food.
source: Such a mechanism with conserved functions enhances survival in wild environments by discriminating against low-quality food.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the evolutionary significance of the identified mechanism.

claim: The intestinal process may be evolved specifically to detect the deficiency of specific nutrients such as vitamins that elude the neuronal sensory system.
source: The intestinal process may be evolved specifically to detect the deficiency of specific nutrients such as vitamins that elude the neuronal sensory system that may be honed to detect the presence of major nutrients and toxins (Bargmann, 1997; Chandrashekar et al., 2006; Watson et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the evolutionary role of the intestinal sensing mechanism.

claim: Intestinal deficiencies in certain fatty acids and pyrimidine are also sensed by signaling systems in C. elegans to alter reproductive/developmental programs.
source: In addition to VB2, we have recently shown that intestinal deficiencies in certain fatty acids and pyrimidine are also sensed by signaling systems in C. elegans to alter reproductive/developmental programs (Chi et al., 2016; Kniazeva et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent published work by the authors.

claim: The protective response to nutrient deficiency by the intestine-initiated mechanism commonly includes regulation of developmental/reproductive programs, in addition to food behaviors.
source: These examples also suggest that the protective response to nutrient deficiency by the intestine-initiated mechanism commonly includes regulation of developmental/reproductive programs, in addition to food behaviors.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the current study and previous work.

claim: VB2 deficiency likely affects the functions of a large number of flavoproteins involved in many essential cellular functions.
source: VB2 deficiency likely affects the functions of a large number of flavoproteins involved in many essential cellular functions; the responses by TORC1, including protease regulation and developmental arrest, may be considered the last and emergent protective actions by the animal.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the known role of VB2 in flavoprotein function.

claim: The responses by TORC1, including protease regulation and developmental arrest, may be considered the last and emergent protective actions by the animal.
source: VB2 deficiency likely affects the functions of a large number of flavoproteins involved in many essential cellular functions; the responses by TORC1, including protease regulation and developmental arrest, may be considered the last and emergent protective actions by the animal.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the biological significance of the TORC1 response.

claim: This study may be the first to connect TORC1 sensing to a specific micronutrient in a model organism.
source: Moreover, our study may be the first to connect TORC1 sensing to a specific micronutrient in a model organism.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the study.

claim: The versatility of TORC1 in responding to the deficiency of multiple nutritional/metabolic inputs suggests that the TORC1-protease pathway may be used to evaluate the levels of multiple essential nutrients in food sources.
source: The versatility of TORC1 in responding to the deficiency of multiple nutritional/metabolic inputs suggests that the TORC1-protease pathway may be used to evaluate the levels of multiple essential nutrients in food sources, albeit that the evaluation process for other nutrients in the intestine remain to be demonstrated in vivo.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the broader implications of the findings.

claim: This study may indicate the importance of live bacteria in providing micronutrients, such as VB2, to animals.
source: This study may also indicate the importance of live bacteria in providing micronutrients, such as VB2, to animals and may thus be highly related to human health, as we obtain vitamins from gut microbes in addition to food sources (Albert et al., 1980; LeBlanc et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the broader implications of the findings for human health.

claim: Humans obtain vitamins from gut microbes in addition to food sources.
source: This study may also indicate the importance of live bacteria in providing micronutrients, such as VB2, to animals and may thus be highly related to human health, as we obtain vitamins from gut microbes in addition to food sources (Albert et al., 1980; LeBlanc et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: VB2 is known to be light sensitive and heat labile in aqueous solution.
source: Since VB2 is known to be light sensitive and heat labile in aqueous solution (Sheraz et al., 2014), the contribution of VB2 from gut microbes could be significantly undervalued.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: The contribution of VB2 from gut microbes could be significantly undervalued.
source: Since VB2 is known to be light sensitive and heat labile in aqueous solution (Sheraz et al., 2014), the contribution of VB2 from gut microbes could be significantly undervalued.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the properties of VB2.

claim: The system used in this study for analyzing VB2 may potentially be effective to investigate the roles and sensing mechanisms for other micronutrients provided by microbes.
source: The system used in this study for analyzing VB2 may potentially be effective to investigate the roles and sensing mechanisms for other micronutrients provided by microbes.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the potential applications of the study system.

claim: VB2 level critically impacts food uptake and foraging behavior by regulating specific protease gene expression and intestinal protease activity.
source: We have established a system to analyze the intestinal response to vitamin B2 (VB2) deficiency in Caenorhabditis elegans, and demonstrated that VB2 level critically impacts food uptake and foraging behavior by regulating specific protease gene expression and intestinal protease activity.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings from the abstract.

claim: This impact is mediated by TORC1 signaling through reading the FAD-dependent ATP level.
source: We show that this impact is mediated by TORC1 signaling through reading the FAD-dependent ATP level.
evidence: This is a summary of the mechanistic findings from the abstract.

claim: The study uncovers a VB2-sensing/response pathway that regulates food-uptake in live animals.
source: Thus, our study in live animals uncovers a VB2-sensing/response pathway that regulates food-uptake, a mechanism by which a common signaling pathway translates a specific nutrient signal into physiological activities, and the importance of gut microbiota in supplying micronutrients to animals.
evidence: This is a summary of the main conclusions from the abstract.

claim: The study demonstrates a mechanism by which a common signaling pathway translates a specific nutrient signal into physiological activities.
source: Thus, our study in live animals uncovers a VB2-sensing/response pathway that regulates food-uptake, a mechanism by which a common signaling pathway translates a specific nutrient signal into physiological activities, and the importance of gut microbiota in supplying micronutrients to animals.
evidence: This is a summary of the main conclusions from the abstract.

claim: The study demonstrates the importance of gut microbiota in supplying micronutrients to animals.
source: Thus, our study in live animals uncovers a VB2-sensing/response pathway that regulates food-uptake, a mechanism by which a common signaling pathway translates a specific nutrient signal into physiological activities, and the importance of gut microbiota in supplying micronutrients to animals.
